title: Fragment 31 and Wharton's numbering
short: Wharton's 'Fragment 2' is the poem now numbered fr. 31; it survives because the treatise On the Sublime quotes it, and Catullus adapted it in poem 51.
body: Wharton numbered the fragments after Bergk's edition, so this poem appears as fr. 2; modern editions (Lobel-Page, Voigt) call it fr. 31, the number used in most scholarship. It survives as a quotation in the essay On the Sublime ascribed to Longinus, whose author admired how Sappho gathers the symptoms of passion into one design, 'not one passion, but a congress of passions' in Wharton's paraphrase. The quotation breaks off after the first line of a fifth stanza, which is why Wharton's version ends in mid-sentence. The translation is Wharton's literal prose of 1885; Catullus 51 and many English versions (Philips, Smollett, Symonds) are printed in his book.

title: peer of gods
greek: φαίνεταί μοι κῆνος ἴσος θέοισιν ἔμμεν' ὤνηρ
short: Greek isos theoisin, 'equal to the gods': the man seems godlike in his good fortune, or in his calm, as he sits beside the girl.
body: The phrase is Homeric (heroes are often 'equal to a god'), and Catullus kept it ('par esse deo'). Readers have argued about why the man is godlike. One view: he is blessed because he is close to the girl. Another: he is godlike because he can sit beside her unmoved, while the speaker collapses; gods, like this man, do not suffer. Wharton's 'peer' (an equal) is an old literary word. 'Seems to me' (phainetai moi) matters too: the poem is about how things appear to the speaker, and the man drops out of view once her own symptoms begin.

title: Who is 'that man'?
short: Critics disagree whether the man is a bridegroom (making the poem a wedding song), a rival, or simply a foil for the speaker's state.
body: Wilamowitz (Sappho und Simonides, 1913) read the poem as a wedding song in praise of a bride and groom; Page (1955) rejected this, finding no sign of a wedding. Many earlier readers took it as a song of jealousy. Some recent critics treat the man as hypothetical ('whoever sits opposite you'), since the Greek relative (ostis) can be generalising. The question is still open, but all readings agree that the poem's centre is not the man but the speaker's experience of seeing and hearing the beloved.

title: sweet speech and lovely laughter
short: The man hears the girl's sweet voice and 'desire-rousing laughter' (gelaisas imeroen); sound, not sight, starts the crisis.
body: Imeroen, 'lovely', comes from himeros, 'desire', so the laughter is literally desire-awakening. Catullus rendered the phrase 'dulce ridentem', and Horace echoed it at the end of Odes 1.22 ('dulce ridentem Lalagen amabo, / dulce loquentem'). The order of the poem is carefully built: hearing (voice, laughter), then seeing ('when I see thee'), then the failure of each sense in turn.

title: flutter
short: Greek eptoaisen, 'set fluttering, scared': a verb of panic and excitement, applied to the heart in the breast.
body: The verb ptoein describes being startled into agitation; it is used in Homer of panic. Placed at the turn from the man to the speaker ('that indeed makes my heart flutter'), it opens the catalogue of symptoms. Wharton's 'flutter' keeps a bird-like image. What 'that' (to) refers to is debated: the girl's laughter, the whole scene, or the man's privileged closeness.

title: the catalogue of symptoms
short: Speech, tongue, skin, eyes, ears, sweat, trembling and colour fail one after another: the most famous description of erotic seizure in Greek.
body: The symptoms move deliberately through the body's senses, as Longinus noticed: soul and body, hearing and tongue, eyes and skin are all affected at once, as though they belonged to someone else (On the Sublime 10). Several symptoms recall Homeric descriptions of fear in battle, so Sappho takes the language of the warrior's terror and applies it to love. George Devereux (1970) read the passage as a clinical anxiety attack; most critics see it as a literary construction. Catullus 51 keeps the sequence but drops the sweat and pallor and ends with a rebuke to himself.

title: my tongue is broken
short: Greek glossa eage, 'my tongue is broken', a famous textual crux: the transmitted words contain an irregular vowel clash and have been doubted.
body: The manuscript of Longinus gives words usually printed as alla kam men glossa eage, 'but my tongue breaks'. The hiatus between glossa and eage is irregular, and editors have proposed emendations (for example a verb meaning 'is frozen' or 'is silent'); others defend the transmitted text, suggesting that the broken sound enacts the broken tongue. Wharton prints and translates the transmitted reading. The image itself, a tongue that snaps like something brittle, is striking and has no close parallel in earlier Greek.

title: a subtle fire has run under my skin
short: Greek lepton pur, 'a thin, delicate fire', running beneath the skin: love as fever.
body: Lepton means 'fine, thin, light'; Wharton's 'subtle' keeps the sense of something that penetrates unseen. Catullus has 'tenuis sub artus / flamma demanat' ('a thin flame runs down beneath my limbs'). Love as fire is a commonplace, but Sappho's emphasis is physical and precise: the fire 'has run under' (hupadedromaken) the skin like a current. Wharton notes that Plutarch called the poem 'mixed with fire'.

title: my ears ring
short: Greek epirrombeisi akouai, 'my ears hum', from rhombos, a spinning top or bull-roarer: a whirring noise that blocks hearing.
body: The verb is connected with rhombos, a whirling ritual instrument that made a humming sound. The image suggests a buzzing that fills the ears, so that hearing, which began the crisis with the girl's voice and laughter, is now blotted out. Catullus: 'sonitu suopte / tintinant aures' ('my ears ring with their own sound'). The detail is one of the most physical in the catalogue, and Wharton's plain 'ring' is accurate.

title: paler than grass
short: Greek chlorotera de poias, 'greener than grass': chloros is the yellow-green pallor of fear or sickness, not simply 'pale'.
body: Chloros, the root of English 'chlorophyll', is the colour of fresh vegetation, of honey, or of sickly skin; Homer speaks of chloron deos, 'green fear' (Iliad 7.479). Wharton's 'paler' is the usual English compromise; some modern translators (Anne Carson among them) keep 'greener than grass'. The comparison ties the body to the natural world and is one of the poem's most-discussed details.

title: little better than one dead
greek: τεθνάκην δ' ὀλίγω 'πιδεύης φαίνομ' ἔμ' αὔτᾳ
short: Greek tethnaken d'oligo 'pideues, 'I seem to fall little short of dying': the climax of the seizure.
body: The speaker sees herself as close to death. Wharton's 'in my madness' has no clear basis in the Greek he prints, which ends the clause with phainomai ('I seem'); modern editions read phainom' em' autai, 'I seem to myself'. That reading stresses that the speaker observes her own collapse: the poem is both an experience of losing control and a cool, exact account of it, a double perspective many critics see as central to its power.

title: But I must dare all, since one so poor
greek: ἀλλὰ πὰν τόλματον, ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα
short: Longinus's quotation breaks off here: 'but all must be dared (or endured), since even a poor man ...'. How the poem continued is unknown.
body: The last line (alla pan tolmaton, epei kai peneta) begins a fifth stanza, but Longinus stops quoting. Tolmaton can mean 'must be dared' or 'must be endured', and peneta, 'a poor man', suggests a general saying, perhaps that even the poor may change their fortune. Some scholars think the poem went on to a reflection that turned the speaker towards endurance or self-command; Catullus ends his version with a stanza rebuking himself for idleness (otium), which may or may not reflect Sappho's lost lines. Wharton's dots mark the gap honestly.
